questions.stem: Pointing to a photograph, Rakesh says, 'She is the daughter of the only son of my grandfather.' How is the woman in the photograph related to Rakesh?

options.option_text: Rakesh's maternal aunt (wife of his mother's brother)
Rakesh's sister (daughter of the same father as Rakesh)
Rakesh's niece (daughter of Rakesh's own sibling)
Rakesh's daughter (born directly to Rakesh himself)

questions.explanation: The only son of Rakesh's grandfather is Rakesh's own father. The daughter of Rakesh's father is Rakesh's sister. Option C (niece) is the classic trap — candidates add an extra generation by reading 'grandfather's son's daughter' as two steps away rather than recognising the chain collapses to the same parental level.

questions.stem: Raman says to Geeta, 'Your only brother's son is my wife's brother.' How is Geeta related to Raman's wife?

options.option_text: Geeta is Raman's wife's mother (who gave birth to her)
Geeta is Raman's wife's paternal aunt (sister of her father)
Geeta is Raman's wife's grandmother (two generations above her)
Geeta is Raman's wife's maternal aunt (sister of her mother)

questions.explanation: Let Geeta's brother be X. X's son Y is Raman's wife's brother, so Raman's wife is also a child of X — making her Geeta's niece. Geeta is therefore Raman's wife's paternal aunt (sister of her father X). Option D (maternal aunt) is the common error: the link passes through Geeta's brother, which is the paternal line of Raman's wife, not the maternal line.

questions.stem: Introducing Kiran, Meena says, 'His mother is the only daughter of my mother.' How is Kiran related to Meena?

options.option_text: Kiran is Meena's brother (they share the same mother)
Kiran is Meena's son (Meena herself is Kiran's mother)
Kiran is Meena's nephew (born to one of Meena's siblings)
Kiran is Meena's grandson (two generations below Meena)

questions.explanation: The only daughter of Meena's mother is Meena herself — a self-referential clue. So Kiran's mother = Meena, making Kiran her son. Option C (nephew) is the dominant trap: candidates assume 'daughter of my mother' must refer to someone other than the speaker, missing that Meena may be the only daughter.

questions.stem: A is the son of B. C is the sister of A. D is the father of C. E is the mother of D. How is B related to E?

options.option_text: B is E's daughter (born directly to E as her child)
B is E's daughter-in-law (married to E's son D)
B is E's granddaughter (two full generations below E)
B is E's sister-in-law (married to one of E's brothers)

questions.explanation: C is A's sister, so they share parents. D is C's father, making D also A's father. B is stated to be A's parent; since D is the father, B must be the mother — and hence D's wife. E is D's mother, so B (D's wife) is E's daughter-in-law. Option A is wrong because B is not E's biological child; she entered the family through marriage to D.

questions.stem: In a coding system: 'A @ B' means A is the father of B; 'A # B' means A is the mother of B; 'A $ B' means A is the brother of B. Which expression correctly means 'X is the maternal uncle of Z'?

options.option_text: X @ Y # Z — making X the maternal grandfather of Z
X $ Y # Z — making X the maternal uncle of Z
X # Y $ Z — making X the maternal grandmother of Z
X $ Y @ Z — making X the paternal uncle of Z

questions.explanation: Maternal uncle = brother of Z's mother. X $ Y means X is Y's brother; Y # Z means Y is Z's mother. Together: X is the brother of Z's mother → maternal uncle. Option D (X $ Y @ Z) makes Y the father of Z, so X becomes the brother of Z's father — that is paternal uncle, the most frequent mix-up in this question type.

questions.stem: In a family of six — P, Q, R, S, T, U — P is married to Q; R is the son of P; T is the daughter of Q; S is the brother of T; U is the son of R. How is U related to S?

options.option_text: U is S's son (born directly to S within this family)
U is S's nephew (U is the son of S's brother R)
U is S's grandson (two full generations below S)
U is S's cousin (born to a sibling of S's parents)

questions.explanation: P and Q are spouses. R is their son; T is their daughter; S is T's brother, so S is also P and Q's child — placing R and S as siblings. U is R's son, making U the nephew of R's sibling S. Option D (cousin) traps candidates who mistakenly assign S to a different parental branch rather than recognising all clues converge on the same P–Q couple.

questions.stem: Pointing to a man in a photograph, a woman says, 'His mother's only brother is the father of my son's only sister.' The woman has exactly one son. How is the woman related to the man?

options.option_text: She is the man's paternal aunt (sister of his father)
She is the man's maternal aunt (wife of his mother's brother)
She is the man's mother (the woman who gave birth to him)
She is the man's sister-in-law (wife of his own brother)

questions.explanation: Since the woman has exactly one son, 'my son's only sister' is the woman's own daughter. 'Father of my daughter' is the woman's husband. The clue then reads: the man's mother's only brother = the woman's husband. So the woman is married to the man's maternal uncle, making her his maternal aunt. Option A (paternal aunt) is the trap for candidates who miss that 'mother's only brother' anchors the relationship firmly on the maternal side.
